title: Sunburst charts: reconcile the leaf ledger before drawing rings
summary: Build a radial hierarchy from one counted leaf ledger, keep parent totals consistent, and make narrow outer sectors inspectable.
body:
Build a radial hierarchy from one counted leaf ledger, keep parent totals consistent, and make narrow outer sectors inspectable.

One record belongs to one leaf

A sunburst partitions a whole into nested categories. The center represents the root, the next ring divides it into top-level groups, and each outward ring divides its parent again. Start from records or an explicitly aggregated leaf ledger, with one complete path per counted item. The same support ticket cannot appear once under Email and again under Chat unless the measure is deliberately ticket-channel events rather than distinct tickets. State that grain next to the chart. A root total of 47 tickets means every first-ring wedge must add to 47, and each branch must equal the sum of its immediate children when the branches represent totals. A separate parent count entered from another report is a common double-counting route. The preparation code below derives parent totals from leaves. Treemaps share the accounting requirement; grain and denominator checks establish what the area means.

Treat absent categories as data, not empty geometry

An incomplete classification is still a counted record. Give it an explicit category such as Unassigned at the first stage where classification is absent, or stop its path at a documented terminal node. Do not distribute its count across known children to make the ring appear complete. If one branch stops at depth two while another reaches depth four, the outer rings describe different levels of detail; the caption must say so. This lesson uses three-level paths so every ticket has the same depth and comparison is direct. Repeated label text in different branches does not imply the same node: the full path is the identifier. For example, Resolved under Email and Resolved under Portal are two separate sectors. Preserve full-path IDs in hover text, exports, and keyboard focus targets. Missingness and export manifests cover the adjoining data contract.

Read angular share against the right parent

A sector's angle communicates its share of the root at its depth, while a child-to-parent percentage answers a different question. Show both numerator and denominator in a tooltip or adjacent table. In the worked ledger, the Support branch contains 33 of 47 tickets, so it spans roughly 253 degrees of the first ring. Within Support, Email accounts for 19 of 33, not 19 of 47. A viewer cannot recover those denominators reliably from a small arc alone. Freeze branch order for repeated reports; re-sorting by the latest count makes equal categories move around the circle between periods. Use a stable color mapping for the first ring, then related shades or labels for descendants. If every small leaf receives a different saturated color, color stops carrying a useful meaning. Stacked bars are often clearer when only two levels matter.

Provide a route out of crowded outer rings

The outer ring can contain dozens of thin sectors even when its parent occupies a generous angle. Do not turn a two-pixel arc into the only way to discover a category. Expose a searchable hierarchy table with full path, count, share of parent and share of root. Keyboard users should be able to enter a branch, inspect children and return to the same focus position. If categories are grouped into Other, define the threshold in counts or root share, retain the original leaves in the downloadable ledger, and never combine categories across different parents merely because their labels match. A sunburst is strongest for following hierarchy and relative composition, not for precise comparison between distant narrow sectors. For precise ranking, pair it with a bar view. Chart accessibility and waffle charts offer alternatives for small shares.

Worked contract

from collections import Counter

def prepare_ticket_sunburst(leaf_ledger):
    totals = Counter()
    if not leaf_ledger:
        raise ValueError("leaf ledger cannot be empty")
    for path, ticket_count in leaf_ledger:
        if (not isinstance(path, tuple) or len(path) != 3 or
                any(not isinstance(label, str) or not label.strip() for label in path) or
                isinstance(ticket_count, bool) or not isinstance(ticket_count, int) or
                ticket_count <= 0):
            raise ValueError("each leaf needs three labels and a positive count")
        for depth in range(4):
            totals[path[:depth]] += ticket_count
    for path, parent_count in totals.items():
        if len(path) == 3:
            continue
        child_sum = sum(count for child, count in totals.items()
                        if len(child) == len(path) + 1 and child[:-1] == path)
        assert parent_count == child_sum
    return totals

ticket_leaves = [
    (("Support", "Email", "Resolved"), 14),
    (("Support", "Email", "Escalated"), 5),
    (("Support", "Chat", "Resolved"), 11),
    (("Support", "Chat", "Escalated"), 3),
    (("Billing", "Portal", "Resolved"), 8),
    (("Billing", "Portal", "Escalated"), 4),
    (("Billing", "Phone", "Unassigned"), 2),
]
totals = prepare_ticket_sunburst(ticket_leaves)
assert totals[()] == 47
assert totals[("Support",)] == 33
assert totals[("Support", "Email")] == 19
assert round(totals[("Support",)] / totals[()] * 360) == 253

Performance and operating cost

Let R be the number of leaf-ledger rows, D the path depth and N the number of distinct hierarchy nodes. Accumulating prefixes takes O(RD) time and O(N) space. The audit loop shown compares each parent with all nodes, so its simple form costs O(N²) time; for a large hierarchy, keep a child-sum counter during the same prefix pass and reduce reconciliation to O(RD + N). The code prepares totals, not drawing coordinates. A renderer assigns a parent interval first, then partitions that interval among children using the derived totals and a fixed category order. It must not sum the root and branch totals again as if each were independent data.

Common Mistakes

  • Counting the same record under multiple leaves without changing the measure definition.
  • Supplying independent parent values that exceed or disagree with their children.
  • Merging identical leaf labels from different parents instead of using full-path IDs.
  • Interpreting a sector's root share as its share of its immediate parent.
  • Leaving narrow outer-ring categories inaccessible without a searchable table.

Validation drill

Build a three-stage classification for 47 customer tickets. Introduce an Unassigned path for records lacking a final outcome, reconcile every parent with its children, and report both parent share and root share for the smallest leaf before drawing any arcs.

title: Sparklines: keep small trends comparable and honest
summary: Prepare compact daily series with a shared value domain, explicit gaps and a text summary before shrinking a chart into a cell.
body:
Prepare compact daily series with a shared value domain, explicit gaps and a text summary before shrinking a chart into a cell.

A compact line still needs a measurement contract

A sparkline removes most visible chart furniture to fit a sequence beside a number or name. The missing axes do not remove the need for units, period, aggregation rule and value domain. If two rows represent daily shipped orders, make the date window identical and disclose whether today's count is final. If one row covers twelve complete days and another covers eleven complete days plus a live partial day, their endpoints are not comparable. Tiny plots are most useful for seeing shape at a glance; the adjacent text should carry the exact latest value, change and time range. Define whether the line connects daily totals, daily averages or cumulative totals. A cumulative series almost always rises and can hide daily reversals. Time-series gaps and seasonal subseries help with period design.

Share the scale when rows are compared

An automatically fitted vertical domain makes every row fill its tiny box, but it can make a calm series look as volatile as one with a one-day spike. If the purpose is comparison across regions, use one locked vertical domain for all regional sparklines with the same unit and period. In the worked data, the shared range runs from nine to 48 shipped orders; East's spike remains visibly larger than West's gradual rise. If the purpose is within-row movement only, row-specific domains can be defensible, but label that choice and do not invite cross-row height comparisons. A zero baseline may be helpful for counts; for rate or temperature series, a domain around the relevant operating range can be better if disclosed. Avoid mixing percentages and counts in one unlabeled column. Axis integrity still applies when the axis is visually absent.

Leave missing days open

An unknown day is neither zero nor a straight bridge between neighbors. The code below returns contiguous observed runs so a renderer draws separate paths and marks the missing slot. It also rejects duplicate or skipped dates, because the positions in a daily sparkline must be equally spaced in calendar time. A sudden line to zero on a day with no data claims an event that was never measured. Connecting across the gap claims continuity that was not observed. If a short gap is deliberately interpolated for display, preserve a gap marker and distinguish the estimated segment with a separate style and text. Highlight an important peak with its value and date, but do not cover the rest of the line with dots. Calendar heatmaps provide a larger view of complete and missing days.

Shrink marks, not interpretation

A 70-pixel chart cannot display hundreds of distinct time positions legibly. For a long series, compute a pixel-column minimum and maximum so a brief spike survives reduction; a single average per column can erase it. Keep first and last observed points, known gaps and annotated events. On mobile, show fewer comparable rows at once rather than forcing labels to microscopic sizes. A text alternative should state the time window, last value, high, low and missing count. If a screen reader must traverse every point, provide an adjacent table or expandable full chart; reading a stream of unlabeled coordinates is not useful. Export the original observations and the reduction method. Level of detail, accessible alternatives and export manifests complete the contract.

Worked contract

from datetime import date, timedelta
from math import isfinite

def prepare_daily_sparklines(regional_series):
    if not regional_series:
        raise ValueError("at least one region is required")
    expected_days = None
    all_values = []
    prepared = {}
    for region, observations in regional_series.items():
        if not region or not observations:
            raise ValueError("region and daily observations are required")
        days = [day for day, _ in observations]
        if (any(not isinstance(day, date) for day in days) or
                any(right - left != timedelta(days=1)
                    for left, right in zip(days, days[1:]))):
            raise ValueError("days must be unique, ordered and consecutive")
        if expected_days is None:
            expected_days = days
        elif days != expected_days:
            raise ValueError("regions must use the same calendar window")
        runs, current = [], []
        for day, value in observations:
            if value is None:
                if current:
                    runs.append(current)
                    current = []
                continue
            if (isinstance(value, bool) or not isinstance(value, (int, float)) or
                    not isfinite(value) or value < 0):
                raise ValueError("daily counts must be finite and nonnegative")
            current.append((day, value))
            all_values.append(value)
        if current:
            runs.append(current)
        prepared[region] = {"runs": runs, "missing": len(days) - sum(map(len, runs))}
    if not all_values:
        raise ValueError("there are no measured values")
    return (min(all_values), max(all_values)), prepared

first_day = date(2026, 4, 6)
east = [12, 14, 13, None, 17, 19, 48, 20, 18, 21, 20, 23]
west = [9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 13, 14, 15, 16, 16, 17, 18]
daily = {"East": list(zip((first_day + timedelta(days=offset)
                            for offset in range(12)), east)),
         "West": list(zip((first_day + timedelta(days=offset)
                            for offset in range(12)), west))}
domain, series = prepare_daily_sparklines(daily)
assert domain == (9, 48)
assert series["East"]["missing"] == 1
assert [len(run) for run in series["East"]["runs"]] == [3, 8]

Performance and operating cost

For S series of T daily slots, validation and run construction take O(ST) time; keeping the plotted observations and gaps takes O(ST) space. The shared domain requires one pass over measured values, not a separate scale fit for every row. On a 70-pixel surface, a renderer should reduce a much longer series by pixel column using extrema and explicit gap flags, then retain the source data for interaction. Do not use a per-column mean when the reader must detect rare spikes; it can remove the very event the compact chart is meant to reveal.

Common Mistakes

  • Letting each row auto-scale while encouraging comparison between rows.
  • Treating a missing daily value as zero or silently connecting across it.
  • Placing rows with different date windows on the same implied horizontal scale.
  • Compressing long data by averages that erase brief maxima or minima.
  • Removing every unit, date and text summary because the chart is small.

Validation drill

Create a grid of 47 daily-order sparklines for equally long periods. Lock a shared range for comparable regions, mark provisional days, count missing slots, and check whether the highest single-day value remains visible after reducing each chart to its final pixel width.

title: Flow maps: separate direction, magnitude and geographic route
summary: Validate a directed movement ledger before drawing arrows, preserve reciprocal flows, and avoid false straight-line paths near the dateline.
body:
Validate a directed movement ledger before drawing arrows, preserve reciprocal flows, and avoid false straight-line paths near the dateline.

A map does not repair a broken movement ledger

A geographic flow map places directed movements between locations. The link may represent shipments, journeys or messages, but it needs a declared unit and time window. Define whether 47 means shipments, parcels, people or distinct vehicles; these are different grains and cannot share a width scale. One record needs a stable origin, destination, direction and nonnegative magnitude. Reciprocal routes are not one undirected line: 47 units eastward and 23 westward have different operational meaning even if they use the same endpoints. Aggregate only records with the same directed pair and compatible time and unit definitions. Compare the sum of mapped links with the source ledger before rendering. Any excluded route, unknown endpoint or local movement needs an explicit count. Sankey reconciliation and directed chord flows expose the same accounting risks without geography.

Treat coordinates as locations, not routes

The endpoints are geographic facts; the line between them is often just a schematic connection. An aircraft, truck or fiber packet may not follow the shortest path. If the chart uses straight projected segments, label them as connections rather than surveyed routes. A great-circle arc gives a spherical shortest connection, yet a map projection bends that arc and may split it at the antimeridian. Drawing a straight line between longitude 179 and longitude minus 178 on a world map can send a three-degree connection almost all the way around the display. The code validates longitude and latitude, computes a wrapped longitude difference and estimates great-circle distance as a diagnostic. It does not claim the movement actually followed that path. Use a projection-aware renderer to interpolate, clip and draw the arc. Dateline handling is required before global deployment.

Encode magnitude without losing the small flows

Arrow width should follow a published scale and unit. Linear width makes a route of 40 units twice as thick as one of 20, but the total ink area also depends on route length; never ask users to infer volume from ink area. If a square-root width scale prevents large links from dominating, say so and show the numeric values beside the map. Two-way traffic needs offset curves, paired arrows or an interactive direction filter so the reciprocal links do not hide each other. Dense hubs can become opaque even when the ledger is correct. Filter by origin, destination or period, then retain the full route table and its total. Grouping minor routes into an unnamed Other line with no endpoint creates a false geographic path. Proportional symbols and linked filters help when destinations crowd together.

Expose the ledger next to the map

A useful flow map includes a table with origin, destination, direction, magnitude, unit, period and any route method. A keyboard user should reach that table without trying to select a hairline arrow. A reader should be able to sort by largest flow and see the same filters that shaped the map. If positions are deliberately jittered to separate overlapping links, keep the true coordinates in the export and say that the display geometry was adjusted. Do not publish precise coordinates for sensitive facilities when aggregated regions answer the question; the mapped grain itself is a disclosure choice. For before-and-after comparisons, freeze the projection, viewport and width scale so movement in the graphic reflects changed data rather than changed camera settings. Accessible chart controls and export manifests cover the delivery layer.

Worked contract

from collections import Counter
from math import asin, cos, isfinite, radians, sin, sqrt

def prepare_transfer_flows(sites, transfers):
    if not sites or not transfers:
        raise ValueError("sites and transfers are required")
    for site, point in sites.items():
        if (not site or not isinstance(point, tuple) or len(point) != 2 or
                any(isinstance(value, bool) or not isinstance(value, (int, float))
                    or not isfinite(value) for value in point) or
                not -180 <= point[0] <= 180 or not -90 <= point[1] <= 90):
            raise ValueError(f"invalid coordinate: {site}")
    directed = Counter()
    for origin, destination, units in transfers:
        if (origin not in sites or destination not in sites or origin == destination or
                isinstance(units, bool) or not isinstance(units, int) or units <= 0):
            raise ValueError("invalid directed transfer")
        directed[(origin, destination)] += units
    routes = []
    for (origin, destination), units in sorted(directed.items()):
        west_lon, west_lat = sites[origin]
        east_lon, east_lat = sites[destination]
        delta_lon = ((east_lon - west_lon + 180) % 360) - 180
        delta_lat = east_lat - west_lat
        arc = sin(radians(delta_lat) / 2) ** 2 + (
            cos(radians(west_lat)) * cos(radians(east_lat)) *
            sin(radians(delta_lon) / 2) ** 2)
        distance_km = 2 * 6371.0088 * asin(min(1.0, sqrt(arc)))
        routes.append((origin, destination, units, round(distance_km, 1)))
    assert sum(route[2] for route in routes) == sum(row[2] for row in transfers)
    return routes

sites = {"West sensor": (179, -17), "East sensor": (-178, -16),
         "Inland hub": (-176, -15)}
transfers = [("West sensor", "East sensor", 31),
             ("West sensor", "East sensor", 16),
             ("East sensor", "West sensor", 23),
             ("West sensor", "Inland hub", 11)]
routes = prepare_transfer_flows(sites, transfers)
assert sum(route[2] for route in routes) == 81
assert any(route[:3] == ("West sensor", "East sensor", 47) for route in routes)
assert any(route[:3] == ("East sensor", "West sensor", 23) for route in routes)

Performance and operating cost

With E transfer rows and V site records, coordinate checks and directed aggregation take O(V + E) expected time and O(V + R) space, where R is the number of unique directed pairs. Sorting the aggregated pairs for stable export adds O(R log R) time. The distance calculation is constant work per pair and is only a spherical diagnostic, not an observed itinerary. The worked ledger totals 81 units across three directed routes, including 47 eastward and 23 westward between the same two sites. A projection-aware drawing library still has to sample and clip each route according to the chosen map projection.

Common Mistakes

  • Combining reciprocal movements into one undirected route.
  • Drawing a long straight line across the map when a short connection crosses the dateline.
  • Calling a schematic or great-circle connector the observed travel path.
  • Changing arrow-width scale between panels while comparing periods.
  • Dropping unknown endpoints or self-movements without reconciling the excluded total.

Validation drill

Take 47 directed dispatch records, including reverse movements and a route near the antimeridian. Reconcile the displayed sum with the ledger, label the connection method, and provide a sortable route table before adding arrow geometry.

  • Chord diagrams: audit directed flows before drawing ribbons
  • Interactive charts: make selection work without a pointer

body:
Choose charts from the question, unit, denominator, and uncertainty the reader needs to judge.

Where to begin

Start with the decision a reader must make. Then choose an encoding that preserves the relevant comparison, define the aggregation grain, and check scale, distribution, small samples, accessibility, and dashboard provenance. The linked project turns those choices into a reviewable operations display.

Read the track

  • Data Visualization Tutorial

  • Aggregation grain and denominator: make every plotted mark auditable
  • Axis scales, baselines and labels: prevent a correct number from telling a false story
  • Distribution plots: keep the tail, missing values and bin policy visible
  • Uncertainty on charts: show denominators and intervals beside estimates
  • Accessible charts: encode meaning without relying on color alone

  • Project: build an auditable receipt-review dashboard
  • Data Visualization: Projects

Choose the right method

A chart with many filters can become expensive to compute and hard to interpret. Pre-aggregate only at a grain that preserves the intended question, and state when a denominator or sample size changes under a filter.

Common Mistakes

Do not truncate an axis without making the effect visible. Color alone must not carry status, and a tidy dashboard does not prove that its source query is correct.

title: Treemaps: validate hierarchy and leaf totals before assigning area
summary: Prevent duplicated parent values, unstable tiles and tiny unreadable leaves.
body:
Prevent duplicated parent values, unstable tiles and tiny unreadable leaves.

Area is a sum contract

A treemap divides a rectangle into nested areas proportional to a nonnegative measure. To compare storage used by product teams, assign each leaf one value and derive parent totals from those leaves. If a parent row already contains the total, summing it with its children doubles the area. Validate that every leaf has one parent, that the hierarchy has no cycle, and that the root total agrees with the source. Grain checks protect the basic unit before layout begins.

Labels cannot rescue tiny tiles

A rectangle's area is hard to estimate precisely, and small leaves cannot hold readable text. Use the treemap for broad composition and a sorted table or bar view for exact comparison. Group genuinely small categories into a named remainder only when their combined value and membership are reported. Do not simply omit leaves to make labels fit. Stacked bars often work better when the hierarchy has only one level or exact cross-category comparison matters.

Keep identity across versions

Many tiling algorithms can rearrange rectangles after a small value change. A user comparing two snapshots may see tiles move and mistake movement for a new category. Use stable IDs, a declared sort and a layout method chosen for the comparison task. If two versions must be compared, consider a fixed hierarchy with an accompanying difference bar; do not imply that a tile's new screen position has meaning. Shared-scale panels help only when the same root total basis is explicit.

Separate structure from measure

Zero-value leaves may be valid members of the hierarchy but have no visible area. Missing measures are different: they should be counted and surfaced outside the tiled display. A negative measure cannot be represented as area without a different visual contract. Tooltips should show path, leaf value, parent total and share; keyboard users need an ordered text tree or table. Accessible text can retain the small leaves that the drawing cannot label.

Worked contract

def hierarchy_totals(
    parent_of: dict[str, str | None], leaf_values: dict[str, int]
) -> dict[str, int]:
    internal = {parent for parent in parent_of.values() if parent is not None}
    if set(leaf_values) != set(parent_of) - internal or any(value < 0 for value in leaf_values.values()):
        raise ValueError("invalid leaf value")
    if any(parent is not None and parent not in parent_of for parent in parent_of.values()):
        raise ValueError("unknown parent")
    for start in parent_of:
        seen = set()
        node = start
        while node is not None:
            if node in seen:
                raise ValueError("cycle in hierarchy")
            seen.add(node)
            node = parent_of[node]
    totals = {node: 0 for node in parent_of}
    for leaf, value in leaf_values.items():
        node = leaf
        while node is not None:
            totals[node] += value
            node = parent_of[node]
    return totals

tree = {"all": None, "support": "all", "mobile": "support",
        "web": "support", "payments": "all"}
totals = hierarchy_totals(tree, {"mobile": 47, "web": 81, "payments": 31})
assert totals["support"] == 128 and totals["all"] == 159

Performance and operating cost

For V nodes, L leaves and maximum depth H, cycle validation and ancestor accumulation take O((V + L)H) time and O(V + H) space for totals and one ancestor set. A deep or very large hierarchy should validate and sum in one postorder pass, O(V). Production layout adds sorting, tiling and label placement. Every terminal node needs a nonnegative measure for area encoding.

Common Mistakes

  • Adding stored parent totals to leaf values and doubling displayed area.
  • Treating zero-area leaves as nonexistent members.
  • Reading a tile move between snapshots as a change in business structure.
  • Dropping tiny categories without reporting the remainder.

Validation drill

Build a three-level storage hierarchy with 47 leaves. Insert one duplicate parent total, one missing measure and one cycle; reject each before rendering, then compare the resulting treemap with a sorted leaf table.

title: Aggregation grain and denominator: make every plotted mark auditable
summary: A visual aggregate is trustworthy only when each source row, grouping key and denominator have a declared meaning.
body:
A visual aggregate is trustworthy only when each source row, grouping key and denominator have a declared meaning.

Fix the source grain

A receipt table can contain one row per receipt while a status log contains several rows per receipt. Joining them and counting rows creates a review volume that rises when the workflow emits more events. Reduce the log to one terminal outcome per receipt before joining, or build an explicit event-level chart. Join cardinality is a precondition for visual accuracy.

Choose the denominator

A chart titled “review completion rate” needs a rule for receipts that were submitted but not yet eligible, rejected at intake or still open. Keep numerator and denominator alongside the plotted rate in the data contract. When filtering by channel, recompute both counts for the filtered cohort; never filter precomputed overall rates and average them.

Control time bins

A daily chart needs one time zone, one interval convention and an explicit policy for late events. A receipt submitted at 23:58 and completed after midnight might belong to the submission-day cohort even though its completion event occurs next day. Calendar policy keeps those two clocks apart. Document whether incomplete days are omitted or shown as provisional.

Reconcile the visual

For two channels with 34 of 47 and 18 of 23 timely receipts, the combined rate is 52 of 70, about 74.3 percent. The simple average of the two channel percentages is different. Test that the dashboard total uses summed counts. Include an empty group and one duplicated receipt ID to catch silent inflation.

Implementation

def weighted_completion_rate(channel_counts):
    timely = 0
    eligible = 0
    for timely_count, eligible_count in channel_counts:
        if not 0 <= timely_count <= eligible_count:
            raise ValueError("invalid channel counts")
        timely += timely_count
        eligible += eligible_count
    return None if eligible == 0 else timely / eligible

Performance and operating cost

Aggregating N rows by C keys is O(N) expected time and O(C) state with a hash map. Sorting labels adds O(C log C). A database group-by can move the work closer to the source, but its join and filter contracts still need inspection.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not average percentages when group sizes differ.
  • Do not count event rows as independent receipts.
  • Do not combine submission and completion timestamps without a cohort rule.

title: Stacked bars: separate composition from volume and preserve denominators
summary: Use absolute and normalized stacks for different questions, and retain every segment count.
body:
Use absolute and normalized stacks for different questions, and retain every segment count.

A stack has two possible questions

An absolute stacked bar shows a total and its parts in the same unit. A normalized bar forces every total to one and shows the mix instead. These are not interchangeable. If depot A closes 47 of 81 requests while depot B closes 470 of 810, both have the same closed share, but the latter carries ten times the workload. Place total and share in adjacent views when both matter. Define the denominator before calculating either bar. The title should say whether the horizontal extent means requests or a fraction of eligible requests.

Keep categories stable

Assign each status one color and one position across periods. If a status disappears, retain its zero-valued place in the data contract rather than shifting every later segment. The unanchored middle segments in a stack are difficult to compare precisely; when one category is the focus, use a grouped bar or a separate trend. Sort bars by a declared metric, such as eligible volume, and keep that order fixed across comparison panels. Facet ordering follows the same rule.

Handle absent and ineligible records

A missing status is not necessarily a measured zero. If the warehouse omits unresolved requests, a normalized stack can show an apparently perfect closure rate even as the unobserved group grows. Reconcile segment counts to the cohort total, expose an unknown state, and reserve a separate no-exposure state when the denominator is zero. A percentage bar for zero eligible requests has no defined composition. Missing-state display should use a label or pattern in addition to color.

Audit every filter

When a dashboard filters by region or week, recompute each segment count from the selected cohort and normalize only after filtering. Do not average prior percentages. Tooltips and exports should include segment count, denominator and percentage; rounded shares may sum to 99.9 or 100.1, which is a display effect rather than a data error. Linked selections must update totals and segments together. Test one-bar, zero-cohort and category-absent states before release.

Worked contract

def composition_by_depot(
    counts: dict[str, dict[str, int]], statuses: tuple[str, ...]
) -> dict[str, dict[str, tuple[int, float | None]]]:
    if len(set(statuses)) != len(statuses) or not statuses:
        raise ValueError("statuses must be unique and nonempty")
    result = {}
    for depot, segments in counts.items():
        if set(segments) - set(statuses) or any(value < 0 for value in segments.values()):
            raise ValueError("unknown status or negative count")
        total = sum(segments.values())
        result[depot] = {
            status: (segments.get(status, 0),
                     segments.get(status, 0) / total if total else None)
            for status in statuses
        }
    return result

mix = composition_by_depot(
    {"north": {"closed": 47, "pending": 34},
     "south": {"closed": 470, "pending": 340}},
    ("closed", "pending", "unknown"))
assert mix["north"]["closed"] == (47, 47 / 81)
assert mix["south"]["closed"] == (470, 470 / 810)
assert mix["north"]["unknown"] == (0, 0.0)

Performance and operating cost

For D depots, S declared statuses and M supplied segment values, validation and construction take O(M + DS) expected time and O(DS) output space. Reusing a prebuilt status set removes repeated set construction in a larger implementation. Rendering a normalized bar still needs the absolute counts for labels and audit. The example treats an absent segment as observed zero only under the stated complete-status contract; without that contract, an absent segment must be marked unknown.

Common Mistakes

  • Reading equal-width normalized bars as equal workloads.
  • Dropping unresolved statuses before calculating shares.
  • Changing stack order between weeks and implying a category moved.
  • Averaging percentages instead of adding segment counts first.

Validation drill

Prepare 13 weekly depot bars with different cohort sizes. Show absolute and normalized versions, then remove one status record from a source extract and verify reconciliation fails rather than silently improving a percentage.

title: Waffle charts: allocate whole cells without losing the total
summary: Turn category counts into a fixed grid with an exact denominator, deterministic remainder allocation and labels that preserve small groups.
body:
Turn category counts into a fixed grid with an exact denominator, deterministic remainder allocation and labels that preserve small groups.

A cell is a share, not necessarily a record

A waffle chart represents parts of one whole using a fixed grid of equal-sized cells. A 10-by-10 grid has one hundred visual units; when the underlying cohort contains 83 tickets, one cell represents roughly 0.83 ticket's worth of share, not a literal individual ticket. Say what the whole is and whether every category is mutually exclusive and exhaustive. If the same ticket can be both pending and escalated, it cannot be counted in both cells of a simple part-to-whole grid without an explicit overlap rule. Use a bar chart when precise rank or a small difference matters more than the visual composition. A waffle grid is useful when readers need a quick impression of shares and an adjacent exact-count table is available. Stacked bars, mosaic plots and denominator rules provide useful comparisons.

Allocate a fixed cell budget once

Each category's ideal cell count is its exact count divided by the total, multiplied by the grid size. Independent rounding can produce a grid with 99 or 101 cells. The worked contract first grants each category the floor of its ideal quota, then distributes the remaining cells to the largest fractional remainders. Ties break by the input category order, which is part of the published contract. This guarantees that cell counts sum to the grid size while keeping each allocation near its quota. The categories stay in a stable semantic order rather than sorting by current size on each refresh. If the whole is zero, there is no share to plot; display an empty state instead of a blank grid that could be read as zero in every category. Cumulative categories and scale rules help keep the total visible.

Keep rare groups visible in text

A category below one cell's share may legitimately receive zero colored cells after allocation. Hiding it from the legend would turn a rounding choice into a false claim that the group does not exist. Label every nonzero category with its exact count and percentage, and disclose the cell value. For operational failures, consider a separate rare-case list or a bar chart if one missed record is consequential. More cells improve resolution but make the grid harder to scan on a phone; choose the budget from the question and display size, not from the desire to show every fractional percent. Do not draw a half-filled cell unless its encoding is explained. Multiple waffle charts need the same cell budget, category order and color mapping, and their raw population totals should appear beside each grid. Text alternatives and detail limits protect readers from hidden exceptions.

Make layout and interaction deterministic

A row-major grid fills cells across a row before moving down. A column-major grid produces a different visual boundary; neither changes the counts, but changing the rule between panels can make categories look shifted. Publish rows, columns, fill order and category order. The contract below returns a complete two-dimensional cell ledger so a renderer can color it without recalculating shares. Keyboard or screen-reader output should provide one summary per category instead of announcing one hundred indistinguishable squares. Hovering a cell should describe the category share and exact count, not pretend that a rounded cell corresponds to a particular ticket. When dashboard filters change the cohort, recompute every allocation from the filtered counts and update the denominator in the same transaction. Linked filters, keyboard access and export contracts complete that behavior.

Worked contract

def allocate_ticket_waffle(category_counts, rows: int, columns: int):
    if (not isinstance(rows, int) or isinstance(rows, bool) or rows < 1 or
            not isinstance(columns, int) or isinstance(columns, bool) or columns < 1):
        raise ValueError("grid dimensions must be positive integers")
    if not category_counts:
        raise ValueError("at least one category is required")
    names = [name for name, _ in category_counts]
    if len(set(names)) != len(names) or any(not name for name in names):
        raise ValueError("category names must be unique and nonempty")
    if any(not isinstance(count, int) or isinstance(count, bool) or count < 0
           for _, count in category_counts):
        raise ValueError("counts must be nonnegative integers")
    total = sum(count for _, count in category_counts)
    if total == 0:
        raise ValueError("a zero-size cohort has no shares")
    cell_budget = rows * columns
    floors = [count * cell_budget // total for _, count in category_counts]
    remainders = [count * cell_budget % total for _, count in category_counts]
    extra = cell_budget - sum(floors)
    for index in sorted(range(len(names)), key=lambda index: (-remainders[index], index))[:extra]:
        floors[index] += 1
    grid = [name for name, cells in zip(names, floors) for _ in range(cells)]
    return dict(zip(names, floors)), [grid[offset:offset + columns]
                                      for offset in range(0, cell_budget, columns)]

ticket_counts = [("resolved", 47), ("pending", 29), ("escalated", 7)]
allocation, grid = allocate_ticket_waffle(ticket_counts, rows=10, columns=10)
assert allocation == {"resolved": 57, "pending": 35, "escalated": 8}
assert len(grid) == 10 and all(len(row) == 10 for row in grid)
assert sum(allocation.values()) == 100

Performance and operating cost

For K categories and C cells, exact integer quotas take O(K) time, sorting remainders takes O(K log K), and constructing the cell ledger takes O(C). Space is O(K + C). The sample has 83 tickets: 47 resolved, 29 pending and 7 escalated. In a one-hundred-cell grid, the largest-remainder rule assigns 57, 35 and 8 cells. Those figures total exactly one hundred, but their displayed cell counts are rounded shares of the 83-ticket cohort. The exact counts stay in the legend and export. If the escalated group had fewer than one cell's share, its nonzero count would still need a label even if the allocation gave it no cell.

Common Mistakes

  • Rounding every category independently and drawing a grid with too many or too few cells.
  • Describing each square as one record when the cohort size differs from the cell budget.
  • Dropping a nonzero category from the legend because it received zero rounded cells.
  • Comparing grids with different cell budgets or changing category colors between panels.
  • Counting overlapping categories twice without defining a mutually exclusive partition.

Validation drill

Create two ten-by-ten grids for weekly ticket cohorts of 83 and 47. Reconcile the category counts to each cohort total, allocate cells with one frozen rule, list any nonzero category that receives no cell, and compare the result with a labeled stacked bar.

title: Time-series charts: distinguish missing days, zeros and provisional periods
summary: Build a complete display calendar, preserve gaps, and label the clocks behind each point.
body:
Build a complete display calendar, preserve gaps, and label the clocks behind each point.

A line implies continuity

A time-series chart maps measurements to ordered instants or calendar periods. Connecting two observed points across an unobserved day implies a path that was never measured. A recorded zero is different: it says the instrument or process observed the period and counted none. Store both the period key and an observation-status field before drawing the line. The observation calendar defines which periods were expected. Use a visible break, hollow mark, or separate missingness strip when a period has no measurement; do not silently replace it with zero.

Name the two clocks

Operational data often has an event timestamp and a processing timestamp. A refund received late may belong to Tuesday's customer cohort but be visible only on Thursday's dashboard. Choose the clock that answers the chart's question and label it in the axis or subtitle. When bucketing timestamps into local days, choose one time zone and convert before taking the date. Daylight-saving changes make a local day shorter or longer than 24 hours in some regions. An elapsed-duration chart should use instants; a calendar-day chart should use dates in the declared zone.

Mark provisional periods

A current day is incomplete even when its count is known so far. Drawing it with the same line and scale as closed days invites a false decline. Carry a finalized flag from the data source, and either exclude the open interval or render it with a different stroke and an explicit as-of time. Late corrections can reopen an earlier point, so the chart's data-version label matters. A reader must know whether yesterday is final, not only whether the plotting job ran.

Protect the comparison

Never join lines across a product outage, a changed population, or a denominator change without an annotation or split. Keep the y-axis unit and calculation stable across the displayed range. If one week contains 42, 47 and 51 eligible cases while the next has a different intake rule, raw counts compare different populations. The aggregation contract should produce both numerator and denominator where a rate is intended. A moving average may reduce noise, but its window, edge behavior and missing-day policy must be stated.

Check the drawn output

Test an interior missing day, an observed zero, an incomplete final day, a late revision, and a daylight-saving boundary for the region being displayed. Confirm that hover text, downloadable data and the axis all use the same period key. A chart-library setting that connects nulls can undo a carefully prepared missingness contract. Inspect the rendered image, not only the input array. The text alternative should report the gap and the as-of timestamp too.

Worked contract

from datetime import date, timedelta

def complete_daily_series(observed: dict[date, int],
                          start: date, end: date) -> list[tuple[date, int | None]]:
    if end < start or any(count < 0 for count in observed.values()):
        raise ValueError("invalid date range or count")
    if any(day < start or day > end for day in observed):
        raise ValueError("observation outside display range")
    return [(start + timedelta(days=offset),
             observed.get(start + timedelta(days=offset)))
            for offset in range((end - start).days + 1)]

points = complete_daily_series(
    {date(2026, 8, 11): 47, date(2026, 8, 13): 0},
    date(2026, 8, 11), date(2026, 8, 13))
assert [count for _, count in points] == [47, None, 0]

Performance and operating cost

For D expected periods and O observed keys, validation plus calendar completion takes O(D + O) time and O(D) output space. The code assumes an already chosen calendar zone and one authoritative count per day. Converting event timestamps and resolving duplicates belong upstream. For a long history, query only the visible interval, and keep finalization state beside each point; creating a million empty periods in a browser is a serving error, not a charting technique.

Common Mistakes

  • Converting an unobserved period into zero and drawing a continuous line.
  • Bucketing by server time zone while labeling the axis with the user's local dates.
  • Treating today's partial count as a completed daily value.
  • Using a rolling average without showing its window and missing-period rule.

title: Large chart series: reduce marks without erasing spikes
summary: Choose a visible-resolution data product and preserve first, last, minimum and maximum values in each bucket.
body:
Choose a visible-resolution data product and preserve first, last, minimum and maximum values in each bucket.

More samples than pixels need a display rule

A line chart with hundreds of thousands of readings across a 900-pixel plot cannot show each reading distinctly. Sending every point still costs transfer, parsing, memory, layout and interaction time. A random sample or every-50th-point stride can erase a brief but operationally important spike. Decide whether the reader is inspecting shape, extrema, exact intervals or anomalies. The chart task determines the reduction method. The full-resolution data remains the source; the plotted series is a deliberately derived view.

Preserve a bounded envelope

For each time bucket, retain its first, last, minimum and maximum observations, ordered by timestamp and deduplicated by identity. This keeps endpoints connected and exposes local peaks and troughs that a mean would smooth away. It is not lossless: the order of several internal turns and narrow oscillations may still be compressed. Show the bucket width or resolution when it affects interpretation, and fetch raw samples on zoom or request. If missing intervals exist, split segments before reducing; joining across a gap creates a fictional line. Gap policy applies before level of detail.

Build levels against stable data versions

Precomputed hourly, daily or pixel-width buckets must use a fixed time origin and a named aggregation function. If a late event revises an old bucket, invalidate that level together with raw data. Cache keys need range, resolution, filters, unit and source generation. A multi-resolution chart can request a coarser level during pan, then replace it with fine points after the interaction settles; label provisional rendering when it might change a decision. Serving freshness constrains what a pre-aggregated chart can claim.

Keep exactness available

Tooltips on reduced marks should describe the bucket, extrema and sample count. Calling a retained minimum a point-in-time average is wrong. A downloadable CSV should offer the filtered raw interval or clearly name the reduced level. If a user clicks a peak to investigate a machine stoppage, resolve it to source IDs rather than an arbitrary nearby display point. The export manifest should state whether the series is raw or reduced.

Measure end-to-end cost

Track transfer bytes, parse time, memory, first paint, pan latency and number of marks actually drawn. A server-side envelope can reduce browser work but adds query and cache-maintenance cost. A canvas renderer can draw many marks faster than DOM-based SVG, yet it needs deliberate keyboard and text alternatives. Test a single-sample range, identical timestamps, gaps and a narrow spike at each bucket boundary. The acceptance check is not only a speedup: the operational alert must remain visible at the default zoom.

Worked contract

def extrema_envelope(samples: list[tuple[int, float]],
                     bucket_size: int) -> list[tuple[int, float]]:
    if bucket_size < 1 or any(samples[index][0] >= samples[index + 1][0]
                               for index in range(len(samples) - 1)):
        raise ValueError("bucket size or time order is invalid")
    reduced = []
    for start in range(0, len(samples), bucket_size):
        bucket = samples[start:start + bucket_size]
        selected = {bucket[0], bucket[-1],
                    min(bucket, key=lambda point: point[1]),
                    max(bucket, key=lambda point: point[1])}
        reduced.extend(sorted(selected, key=lambda point: point[0]))
    return reduced

readings = [(47, 4.0), (48, 4.1), (49, 81.0), (50, 4.2),
            (51, 4.0), (52, 3.9)]
visible = extrema_envelope(readings, 4)
assert (49, 81.0) in visible and visible[0] == readings[0]
assert len(visible) <= 4 * ((len(readings) + 3) // 4)

Performance and operating cost

For N sorted samples and bucket size B, the demonstration runs in O(N + (N/B) log 4) time and emits at most four observations per bucket, O(N/B) output space. Python slices hold up to O(B) temporary items. It assumes strictly increasing timestamps and one continuous segment; production data with same-time events needs an explicit tie policy, and gaps need separate segments. Maintaining a pyramid of levels increases storage but can make viewport requests proportional to visible resolution rather than total history.

Common Mistakes

  • Taking every nth reading and deleting a short-lived alarm spike.
  • Reducing across a missing-data gap and drawing a continuous line.
  • Calling a retained minimum or maximum a bucket average.
  • Caching a reduced level without the filter and source-version keys.

Validation drill

Reduce a 47,000-point sensor series to a 900-pixel view. Insert 19 one-point spikes at varied bucket positions and verify every spike survives the chosen display reduction; compare load and pan times with the raw series.

title: Calendar heatmaps: distinguish an empty day from an absent day
summary: Generate the full date grid, fix the reporting time zone and encode missing observations separately from zero.
body:
Generate the full date grid, fix the reporting time zone and encode missing observations separately from zero.

A blank square has several meanings

A calendar heatmap arranges daily values in a weekly grid. A white day could mean zero events, no feed, a day outside the reporting range or a suppressed value. Those states cannot share one silent color. Generate every expected local date first, then join observations and label each cell's status. Missing-cell heatmaps need the same distinction. For a support operation, a zero confirmed ticket count is evidence; an uncollected Saturday is not. Show the number of complete days beside any annual total.

Choose the reporting day

An event at 00:20 UTC may belong to the prior local day. Convert timestamps to the declared reporting zone before aggregating, and record the zone in the export. Daylight-saving changes produce 23- or 25-hour local days in some regions; counts remain counts, but per-hour rates need an exposure adjustment. A calendar grid without its time-zone contract can move incidents across cells and distort weekday patterns. Time-series calendar rules cover incomplete current periods and delayed arrivals. Mark provisional days rather than painting them as final.

Keep color comparable

Fix the numeric color domain across years or related teams when the goal is comparison. Otherwise each year may assign the darkest shade to a different count. If the distribution has a long tail, state any transform or clipped maximum. A daily rate requires the matching daily denominator; weekend exposure often differs from weekday exposure. Grain and denominator come before color selection. A tooltip should expose date, value, status, denominator if used and refresh time, while a text table remains available for keyboard and screen-reader users.

Week structure is a locale decision

Some audiences expect Monday-first weeks; others expect Sunday-first. Label weekdays, show month boundaries and test leap years, year transitions and ISO week edges. Do not infer a causal weekday pattern from a few colored streaks. A release schedule, holiday closure or data-delivery gap may explain the pattern. Event annotations should state what happened without claiming effect. Export an explicit date-status table so another analyst can reconstruct the image rather than reverse-engineering its colors.

Worked contract

from datetime import date, timedelta

def complete_daily_series(start: date, end: date,
                          observed: dict[date, int | None]
                          ) -> list[tuple[date, str, int | None]]:
    if end < start or any(day < start or day > end for day in observed):
        raise ValueError("dates must fall inside the requested period")
    if any(value is not None and (not isinstance(value, int) or value < 0)
           for value in observed.values()):
        raise ValueError("daily counts must be nonnegative integers")
    result = []
    day = start
    while day <= end:
        value = observed.get(day)
        status = "missing" if value is None else "observed"
        result.append((day, status, value))
        day += timedelta(days=1)
    return result

calendar_rows = complete_daily_series(
    date(2026, 10, 1), date(2026, 10, 4),
    {date(2026, 10, 1): 47, date(2026, 10, 2): 0,
     date(2026, 10, 4): 59})
assert calendar_rows[1] == (date(2026, 10, 2), "observed", 0)
assert calendar_rows[2] == (date(2026, 10, 3), "missing", None)

Performance and operating cost

For D days and O observed keys, validation and completion take O(D+O) time and O(D) output space. This code assumes the input keys already represent the correct reporting-zone dates; timestamp conversion belongs upstream. If a source uses null to mean suppression rather than missing delivery, give it its own status before calling this function. Store daily exposure separately when coloring rates.

Common Mistakes

  • Turning missing days into zeros.
  • Aggregating UTC dates and labeling the result as a local calendar.
  • Allowing each year to auto-scale its colors during comparison.
  • Treating a partly reported current day as final.

Validation drill

Build a 47-day operations calendar with a confirmed zero, a late feed, a holiday closure and one provisional day. Export the four states and explain the color domain.

title: Accessible charts: encode meaning without relying on color alone
summary: A chart needs legible labels, keyboard access where interactive, and a text route to the same substantive data.
body:
A chart needs legible labels, keyboard access where interactive, and a text route to the same substantive data.

Keep meaning redundant

A red and green pair is not enough to distinguish two completion series. Use direct labels, distinct line styles or marker shapes, and a legend that names the measured groups. Color can reinforce meaning but should not carry it alone. Axis labels must include units and remain legible at narrow widths.

Write a useful alternative

An image alternative should state the main comparison and notable exception, not simply “bar chart.” A companion table should expose exact values, periods and denominators for readers who cannot use the graphic. For an interactive chart, its filter controls need visible names, keyboard focus and a text update when the dataset changes.

Test the states

Check high zoom, narrow layout, monochrome output and keyboard-only interaction. A hover tooltip is not an adequate source of the only exact value. If a tooltip reports 74 percent but the accessible table says 73.6 percent, declare rounding once and use it consistently. Dashboard filters must update both representations together.

Budget complexity

A dense chart with 40 small labels may be technically accessible but still hard to scan. Reduce visible series, use a stable sort and provide a drill-down or table for detail. Retain disclosure of hidden groups and totals so simplification does not selectively remove an unfavorable channel.

Implementation

def chart_alt_text(period_label, channel_rates):
    measured = [(channel, rate) for channel, rate in channel_rates.items() if rate is not None]
    if not measured:
        return f"{period_label}: no channel has an eligible denominator."
    highest_channel, highest_rate = max(measured, key=lambda item: item[1])
    return (f"{period_label}: {len(measured)} channels measured; "
            f"{highest_channel} has the highest completion rate at {highest_rate:.1%}.")

Performance and operating cost

A short alternative over C channels costs O(C) time and O(C) temporary space in this implementation. For larger datasets, aggregate once and reuse the exact result for chart, table and alternative text to prevent divergence.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not rely on hue alone to identify a series.
  • Do not put the only exact value in a pointer-only tooltip.
  • Do not write alternative text from stale data after filters change.

title: Map boundaries: handle antimeridian crossings before drawing routes
summary: Normalize longitude, split crossings and treat projection distance as a display property.
body:
Normalize longitude, split crossings and treat projection distance as a display property.

Longitude has a seam

A route from 177 degrees east to 178 degrees west crosses a narrow part of the Pacific. A renderer that simply connects numeric longitudes may draw a line across nearly the entire map. Choose a longitude convention, validate it at ingestion, and split a crossing before sending geometry to the visual layer. Keep the original coordinates as well as display segments. Symbol maps also need a clear coordinate meaning; a route line needs the additional seam rule.

A bounding box can wrap

For an antimeridian-spanning area, a western longitude numerically greater than the eastern longitude can describe a small region. Do not automatically swap the two values or calculate width by direct subtraction. Compute wrapped angular span and tell a mapping library whether its viewport crosses the seam. A naive min-to-max bounding box may zoom to almost the whole world. Region boundaries need the same care when a polygon is split into multiple pieces for display.

Projection changes visual geometry

A flat map projects a curved surface. Pixel distance, area and direction can vary with projection and latitude. Use a projection appropriate to the question, and avoid estimating physical travel distance with screen coordinates. A straight segment drawn in longitude and latitude is not automatically the shortest path on Earth. When a route represents measured travel, retain the actual track; when it represents an abstract connection, label it as such. Scale integrity applies to maps as well as charts.

Preserve identity across pieces

After a crossing is cut into two display segments, both pieces must retain one route ID so a tooltip, filter and export refer to the same underlying trip. A segment count is not a trip count. Include source coordinate order, time zone for event timestamps, geometry version and wrapping method in the export. Test endpoints exactly at positive and negative 180 degrees. The export manifest should record enough to reproduce the same viewport and splitting rule after a map library upgrade.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def split_dateline_segment(west: tuple[float, float],
                           east: tuple[float, float]
                          ) -> list[list[tuple[float, float]]]:
    lon_a, lat_a = west
    lon_b, lat_b = east
    if not all(isfinite(value) for value in (*west, *east)):
        raise ValueError("coordinates must be finite")
    if not (-180 <= lon_a <= 180 and -180 <= lon_b <= 180
            and -90 <= lat_a <= 90 and -90 <= lat_b <= 90):
        raise ValueError("longitude or latitude outside range")
    difference = lon_b - lon_a
    if abs(difference) <= 180:
        return [[west, east]]
    adjusted_b = lon_b - 360 if difference > 180 else lon_b + 360
    seam = -180 if adjusted_b < lon_a else 180
    fraction = (seam - lon_a) / (adjusted_b - lon_a)
    seam_lat = lat_a + fraction * (lat_b - lat_a)
    opposite = 180 if seam == -180 else -180
    return [[west, (seam, seam_lat)], [(opposite, seam_lat), east]]

shipping_route = split_dateline_segment((177, -17), (-178, -18))
assert shipping_route == [
    [(177, -17), (180, -17.6)],
    [(-180, -17.6), (-178, -18)],
]

Performance and operating cost

Splitting one two-point segment is O(1) time and space; a route with N points needs O(N) processing and output. The interpolation is linear in longitude and latitude for display geometry, not a geodesic calculation. For long-distance navigation or polar tracks, densify with a suitable geographic method before projecting. A production pipeline must define how exact-seam endpoints, multi-segment tracks and duplicate 180-degree coordinates are serialized.

Common Mistakes

  • Drawing a nearly global line between two points that are close across the seam.
  • Swapping wrapped bounding-box longitudes and accidentally selecting most of the world.
  • Measuring real distance from flat-map pixels.
  • Counting two rendered pieces as two journeys.

Validation drill

Draw 47 shipping tracks with three seam crossings. Keep one ID per journey, verify wrapped viewport width, and compare the exported track length with the number of display segments.

title: Sankey diagrams: reconcile flows before sizing links
summary: Make every stage transition accountable, including dropouts and unobserved destinations.
body:
Make every stage transition accountable, including dropouts and unobserved destinations.

A link represents a transfer

A Sankey diagram uses link width to encode quantity moving between stages. The visual claim is stronger than a list of counts: a unit leaving one stage must either enter a named next stage, exit the process, or remain unobserved under a declared cutoff. If 81 claims enter triage and 47 reach review, the other 34 need a visible destination, not an unexplained gap. Unit-of-analysis rules prevent one claim with multiple events from becoming several flows.

Give nodes stage-specific identities

The same label at two stages does not necessarily describe the same state. Use stable stage and state IDs, deduplicate by entity and transition, and decide how repeated or backward transitions are handled. A diagram that assumes a directed acyclic process can fail when work returns to triage. In that case, either aggregate one chosen journey window or use another graph view that represents loops. Network diagrams can show cycles, though they answer a different question.

Check conservation at intermediate stages

For a closed interval, incoming and outgoing measured quantities at a transit state should balance after explicit additions, losses and stock change. If 47 enter review and 42 leave, five may still be in progress; add a pending exit or annotate the stock. For a live interval, arrivals and departures can differ because the cohort has not matured. Attach extraction time and observation horizon to the flow, and never compare incoming of one cohort to outgoing of another. Provisional periods need separate handling.

Make ordering and scale inspectable

Link crossing is partly a layout choice. Reordering nodes can reduce crossings without changing the data, so visual proximity must not be treated as a causal relation. Show quantities, units and denominators in text or a companion table. Fixed link colors can track origin across stages, but blending may obscure a small branch; direct labels or hover summaries help. Accessible alternatives should list source, target and value. Large graphs may be better as a transition table.

Worked contract

from collections import defaultdict

def reconcile_flow(
    links: list[tuple[str, str, int]], transit_nodes: set[str]
) -> dict[str, tuple[int, int]]:
    incoming = defaultdict(int)
    outgoing = defaultdict(int)
    for source, target, quantity in links:
        if not source or not target or quantity < 0:
            raise ValueError("invalid flow link")
        outgoing[source] += quantity
        incoming[target] += quantity
    balances = {node: (incoming[node], outgoing[node]) for node in transit_nodes}
    if any(entered != left for entered, left in balances.values()):
        raise ValueError(f"unreconciled transit node: {balances}")
    return balances

journey = [("intake", "review", 47),
           ("intake", "unobserved-exit", 34),
           ("review", "closed", 42),
           ("review", "pending", 5)]
assert reconcile_flow(journey, {"review"}) == {"review": (47, 47)}
assert sum(value for source, _, value in journey if source == "intake") == 81

Performance and operating cost

For E links and T transit nodes, accumulation and reconciliation take O(E + T) expected time and O(V) space for V encountered nodes. Layout can be substantially more expensive and depends on the rendering algorithm; do not mix that cost with the inexpensive accounting check. A real workflow also checks duplicate entity transitions and whether stock change belongs in the diagram. The example treats all links as counts in one cohort and one period.

Common Mistakes

  • Hiding exits to make the main path look complete.
  • Counting multiple events from one entity as separate stage transfers.
  • Balancing one period's arrivals against another period's departures.
  • Assuming node position or link crossing has business meaning.

Validation drill

Model 81 claims through intake, review and closure. Add a pending branch and an unobserved exit; fail the reconciliation when either is removed, then render a transition table beside the flow.

title: Chord diagrams: audit directed flows before drawing ribbons
summary: Turn a directed source-to-destination matrix into an auditable chord layout without hiding self-flows or double-counting totals.
body:
Turn a directed source-to-destination matrix into an auditable chord layout without hiding self-flows or double-counting totals.

Fix the unit and direction first

A chord diagram curls a square flow matrix around a circle. One row identifies the source; one column identifies the destination. A matrix entry can represent parcels moved between depots, but it cannot mix parcel count with shipment value. Decide whether the story is directed before any ribbons are drawn: a transfer from North to East is not the same record as East to North. If the values describe mutual relationships rather than movements, use an undirected contract and explain how two mirrored cells are consolidated. Network graphs emphasize topology; chords emphasize the volume between a manageable set of named groups. Their apparent symmetry can mislead readers when source and destination have different meanings, so label the ends or use a visible directional cue.

Reconcile sectors and ribbons

For a directed matrix, the outbound total of a group is its row sum and inbound total is its column sum. Decide whether each sector encodes outbound alone or inbound plus outbound; otherwise a sector width may appear to contradict its label. The worked contract below reports both. A transfer from a group to itself belongs on the diagonal and must be kept or explicitly excluded. Draw a self-loop distinctly because it can consume a large share of an arc without crossing the center. A ribbon should have an auditable value in an accompanying table. Sankey diagrams are often clearer when a process has ordered stages and conservation across them must be inspected.

Keep categories and filters stable

Arc order changes which ribbons overlap and can make the same data look dense or sparse. Set one documented category order across periods and filtered views. If an unseen group is grouped into Other, publish which group IDs it contains and keep its membership fixed when comparing periods. An interaction should reveal source, destination, amount, unit, time window and whether the value is a self-loop. It should also disclose the current filter cohort. Linked filter state is part of the reading contract: a selected destination must not silently redefine the total behind each sector. Export the full matrix rather than only the visible top ribbons.

Use density as a stopping rule

With 47 groups, there can be 2,209 directed cells before any filtering. Even a complete and accurate chord can become an unreadable knot. Start with a ranked table, a small set of stable groups or a matrix heatmap when precise cell comparisons matter. Heatmaps preserve a fixed row-column grid and make absent flows easier to spot. If the chord is retained, annotate whether zeros mean no observed movement or unavailable data, and provide text alternatives for keyboard and screen-reader access. Test the display at narrow widths; hiding labels does not remove the underlying ambiguity.

Worked contract

def directed_flow_ledger(groups: list[str],
                         flows: dict[tuple[str, str], int]):
    if not groups or len(groups) != len(set(groups)) or any(not name for name in groups):
        raise ValueError("group names must be unique and nonempty")
    known = set(groups)
    if any(source not in known or target not in known or
           type(amount) is not int or amount < 0
           for (source, target), amount in flows.items()):
        raise ValueError("flow endpoints and amounts must be valid")
    matrix = [[flows.get((source, target), 0) for target in groups]
              for source in groups]
    outbound = {source: sum(matrix[index])
                for index, source in enumerate(groups)}
    inbound = {target: sum(matrix[index][column]
                           for index in range(len(groups)))
               for column, target in enumerate(groups)}
    assert sum(outbound.values()) == sum(inbound.values())
    return matrix, outbound, inbound

depots = ["North", "East", "West"]
transfers = {("North", "East"): 47, ("East", "North"): 13,
             ("North", "North"): 5, ("West", "East"): 29}
matrix, outbound, inbound = directed_flow_ledger(depots, transfers)
assert matrix[0] == [5, 47, 0]
assert outbound["North"] == 52
assert inbound["East"] == 76
assert sum(outbound.values()) == 94

Performance and operating cost

For G groups, matrix construction takes O(G²) time and O(G²) space even when most flows are zero. The sparse input map is better for storage and for very large networks; the dense matrix is useful only when the chosen renderer requires it. The ledger counts each directed transfer once, including a self-loop, and proves that aggregate outbound equals aggregate inbound. It does not turn the chart into a conservation model across time: inventory changes and external entries still require their own rows.

Common Mistakes

  • Adding both directions into one ribbon while calling the result directed.
  • Dropping self-loops because they do not cross the circle.
  • Changing arc order or the membership of Other between comparison panels.
  • Treating an unavailable matrix cell as an observed zero.

Validation drill

Audit 59 transfer routes between five depots. Reconcile each outbound and inbound subtotal, then compare a chord with a matrix table at phone width.

title: Proportional-symbol maps: size circles by area, not radius
summary: Declare the location meaning and value unit, then preserve zero, overlap and boundary context.
body:
Declare the location meaning and value unit, then preserve zero, overlap and boundary context.

A symbol has a location contract

A circle over a map may represent a precise facility, a regional centroid or an approximate address. Those are not equivalent. State what the coordinate means and how much location precision the data support. Choropleth maps color whole regions; proportional symbols encode a value at a point or chosen anchor. Do not place a regional total at a centroid without telling the reader that the circle summarizes an area. If location is sensitive, aggregate or coarsen before publication rather than relying on small marker size to conceal it.

Area should represent quantity

If a symbol encodes a nonnegative count, its visual area should be proportional to that count. Doubling the radius multiplies area by four, exaggerating the larger value. Compute radius from the square root of value relative to a declared maximum. Use a visible reference legend with at least two example magnitudes. A zero count should remain a recorded zero, even if its circle has no area; a tiny outline or table entry may be needed to keep the location discoverable. Scale integrity also means fixing the size domain across maps intended for comparison.

Overlapping circles need an explicit policy

Dense areas can hide smaller symbols under larger ones. Drawing order, opacity and zoom can all change what a reader sees. Try smaller maximum radius, outlines, clustering with disclosed counts, or an alternate ranked table. Do not let overlap remove records from the export. Hexbin density may be better when the question is where point events concentrate, while a proportional-symbol map is better when each point already has a meaningful aggregate. Test overlapping facilities at the closest supported zoom and on a narrow phone viewport.

Count and rate are different maps

A large population center may dominate a count map while having a modest per-person rate. A rate can be mapped with symbol size only if the legend names its denominator and the sampling uncertainty is not buried. Often a count-sized symbol plus a separately encoded rate is too much for one map; use paired maps or a table. The denominator contract must follow the geography and period. Export ID, coordinate meaning, count, denominator, computed rate, symbol radius and suppression state, so the map can be checked without its pixels.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite, sqrt

def area_scaled_radii(values: dict[str, float],
                      maximum_radius: float) -> dict[str, float]:
    if not isfinite(maximum_radius) or maximum_radius <= 0:
        raise ValueError("maximum radius must be positive")
    if not values or any(not place for place in values):
        raise ValueError("locations must be named")
    if any(not isfinite(value) or value < 0 for value in values.values()):
        raise ValueError("mapped values must be finite and nonnegative")
    maximum_value = max(values.values())
    if maximum_value == 0:
        return {place: 0.0 for place in values}
    return {place: maximum_radius * sqrt(value / maximum_value)
            for place, value in values.items()}

service_calls = {"north depot": 47, "south depot": 188, "west depot": 0}
radii = area_scaled_radii(service_calls, 20)
assert radii["south depot"] == 20
assert radii["north depot"] == 10
assert radii["west depot"] == 0

Performance and operating cost

For N locations, finding the maximum and calculating radii takes O(N) time and O(N) output space. The code sizes nonnegative values by area and leaves geographic projection, collision handling and legend generation to the map renderer. A production map must keep one fixed reference maximum across views that readers are expected to compare; recalculating it after every filter changes apparent size.

Common Mistakes

  • Making radius proportional to count and thereby exaggerating area.
  • Treating a regional centroid as an exact event location.
  • Letting large symbols cover small ones without a table or overlap strategy.
  • Comparing maps whose size domains were auto-scaled independently.

Validation drill

Map 59 service depots with zero, small and large call counts. Use area-scaled circles, disclose the location meaning and produce a fixed-size legend for two reporting periods.
